subject: Culture
title: Dowry and Bride Price
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Dowry and Bride Price.

hook.text: In South Sudan, a bride can cost 200 cattle. Families go into debt for decades to marry a son.

buildup.text: Bride price transfers wealth to the bride's family. Dowry does the opposite—it flows with the bride.

discovery.text: Both systems tie family honor to the transaction. A low offer insults the bride's kin publicly.

twist.text: India banned dowry in 1961, but enforcement is weak. Dowry disputes still cause thousands of deaths yearly.

climax.text: Where marriage is a contract between families, love is a bonus—not the foundation.

punchline.text: Romance rewrote marriage in some cultures only.

quiz.question: When did India officially ban dowry?

details.summary: Dowry (family pays the groom) and bride price (groom pays the bride's family) are economic transactions embedded in honor systems. Dowry practices in India, despite being illegal since 1961, still drive dowry deaths.
details.whyItMatters: Marriage economics reveal how honor systems commodify women's reproductive capacity. Understanding dowry and bride price explains violence patterns, family debt, and gender inequality in billions of lives.
takeaways: Indian dowry deaths kill thousands of women annually despite legal bans
African bride price treats marriage as an economic contract between families
Both systems tie women's value to their economic contribution to marriage

faq.question: What is the difference between dowry and bride price?
faq.answer: Dowry flows from the bride's family to the groom — payment for 'taking' the daughter. Common in South Asia. Bride price flows from the groom to the bride's family — compensation for 'losing' the daughter. Common in Sub-Saharan Africa.

faq.question: Why do dowry deaths still occur in India?
faq.answer: Despite India's 1961 Dowry Prohibition Act, dowry remains deeply embedded in marriage culture. Families face enormous pressure to provide competitive dowries. When payments are deemed insufficient, brides face harassment, abuse, and murder — often staged as kitchen fires ('stove bursts').
